name: Yetfa
catalog_citation: Donohue, Mark. 2005. Tone and the Trans New Guinea languages. In Shigeki Kaji (ed.), Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-Linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena: Historical Development, Tone-Syntax Interface, and Descriptive Studies (Dec. 14-16, 2004, ILCAA), 33-54. Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. ISBN 4872979176.
catalog_locator: p. 36, footnote 4 (scan page 4 of the author's PDF)
catalog_quote: Since there is such strong evidence of a central cordilleran pattern of pitch utilisation in word-tone systems, with a 'spillover' of pitch-accent to the south, it is surprising that Ross did not examine the languages to the north of the main range. The languages are not part of the TNG family, but are tonal with tone bearing a high contrastive load. Examples of such languages include Yetfa and Lepki, immediately north of, and in contact with, Mek languages from the highlands, and further away Kaure. See Map 3 for a complete picture of tonal patterns in New Guinea.

Footnote 4 on scan page 04 (= p. 36) is in the whole-page scanned extract, last 7 lines: '4 Since there is such strong evidence of a central cordilleran pattern of pitch utilisation in word-ione [scanned for word-tone] systems, with a spillover of pitch accent to the south, it is surprising that Ross did not examine the languages to the north of the main range. The languages are not part of the TNG family, but are tonal with tone bearing a high contrastive load. Examples of such languages include Yetfa and Lepki, immediately north of, and in contact with, Mek lang…
new_statements.relation_note: Explicit claim that Yetfa (with Lepki and Kaure) is tonal with high functional load; no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yetfa is asserted to be a tone language in which tone carries a high contrastive (lexical) load; nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; no data, tone inventory or source for the Yetfa claim is given (the paper is a typological reply to Ross on TNG tone; Yetfa appears only in this footnote and presumably on Map 3, an image not scanned-readable).
new_statements.identity_note: Names 'Yetfa' explicitly, located 'immediately north of, and in contact with, Mek languages' together with Lepki and Kaure -- that is the Yetfa of Pegunungan Bintang/Keerom (yetf1238); no namesake exists. Author-hosted scan (Internet Archive copy of papuan.linguistics.anu.edu.au); the ANU repository copy (hdl 1885/36384) is embargoed until 2037. Found via Google Books volumes-feed snippet of the printed volume (Google Books id MEhiAAAAMAAJ). | Lists 'Biksi (Sepik phylum?)' -- Laycock's Biksi, the PNG-side name of yetf1238 (Glottolog treats Yetfa and Biksi as one language). Author-hosted partial scan (2-up images, no text; journal version paywalled at De Gruyter). scanned of the relevant half-page has the right margin clipped by the gutter; bracketed letters in the quote are restorations of clipped line-ends.

new_statements.quote: 5.4. Languages reported to be or likely to be tonal languages. Many languages are either reported to display tonal behaviour, or ap[pear] from available wordlists to be likely to either use some sort of sup[ra]segmental factors in differentiating words, or to have an unaccountabl[y] large number of homonyms amongst their basic vocabulary. [...] For details of the evidence or reports supporting the claim [that] they might be tonal, see Donohue (1993). The languages thought [to be] tonal include the following: [...] Ningil (To[rricelli] phylum), Biksi (Sepik phylum?), Amto, Musian (Amto-Musian) [...]
